If a clock transition isn't fast enough, you should consider buffering it with a Schmitt trigger based logic chip or buffer.

For example, I made a single pushbutton controlled two light switch with a dual D flip flop chip (state storing), quad Schmitt trigger NAND (switch debouncing, some power-on reset logic, doubled up inputs for inverters). Q' just went back to data, and either Q or Q' became the clock for the second flip flop.

The most challenging part was making the power-on reset work under various conditions: power input slowly rising, quickly rising, partial power-off (voltage never totally disappearing), all these conditions with the debounce capacitor in different states of charge, etc. I ended up using the power indicator LED as part of the power-on reset circuit (as a voltage reference of sorts)... I wish I would have made a schematic of all the weirdness. Anyway, the constraint I worked with is that accidental output activation isn't allowed. It is okay if it loses state and turns both outputs off, but not turning something on that was off, through power glitches.

Anyway, the long and short of it is you can use an RC filter into a Schmitt trigger logic chip and it does a pretty decent job of debouncing. It might not catch some really weird corner cases of very momentary partial contact (the enforced delay between presses might become rather short, but it's still there), but it did perfectly fine with the real switch I had connected to it.

Well, there are a few issues. First, the transformer is putting out alternating current, and probably the direct current fan won't like this much at all. The other problem is that 12V is the "average" voltage put out by the transformer (actually RMS average, which is slightly different and approximates the equivalent AC voltage that a resistive load would respond to the same as 12VDC).

But the second issue is that the peak voltage is at least the square root of 2 times 12V, and maybe a little more if the transformer is specified for voltage under its rated load. It's not unheard of for a transformer like that to put out 25V or a little more peak voltage.

So the answer to the first problem is to use a bridge rectifier. This makes each negative half cycle of AC mirrored so that the output is always positive. If you put a capacitor after the rectifier, it will smooth the output voltage (it will approach the peak voltage of the transformer and dip a little between peaks).

If the transformer had an appropriate peak voltage, this would be enough to end with. But because the peak voltage is higher than would be good to put on the fan, you'll also want a 12V regulator like a common linear voltage regulator (and possibly additionally a small ceramic capacitor to put across its output for stable operation, but you might get away without it in this case).

You want an astable multivibrator.

The short intro to how it works is that the timer IC has an output that drives low or high (you want to take this as your clock output), and then there is an input pin that flips the output when it crosses past a third or two-thirds of the supply voltage. This pin gets connected to a capacitor pin (the other end of the capacitor goes to ground), and you use a resistor from the timer output to the top end of the capacitor, which pulls the capacitor towards the supply voltage or towards ground depending on the output state.

So the capacitor voltage moves by a third of the supply voltage each half cycle (this would likely not be appropriate for a CMOS input in any way, but that's why you use the timer output instead), but that particular voltage swing makes the RC time calculations really nice to work with. Basically, multiply the resistance and capacitance (in ohms and farads), and that's approximately how many seconds it takes for each half cycle. Keep the resistance in the 1K to 100K range for best results, so that it doesn't try to pull too much or too little current (too much is an obvious problem, but with too little, leakages can throw off operation).

Check a relevant electronics resource and scroll down to "50% Duty Cycle Astable" - this is the circuit I'm talking about - many of the examples use two resistors in a different configuration, but for a 50% duty cycle like a normal clock has, there's no need. The capacitor on the control pin might not be necessary depending on the particular timer IC, but it's probably best to include it (it doesn't really factor into the timing calculations though). Hopefully, this helps!

[Edit:] Actually, at 5V operation, you will save a ton of grief by using a CMOS timer instead of a normal one, because the output high voltage may not reach high enough! The one time I implemented this circuit, it was with a CMOS part because it needed to draw very little power during operation (it was part of a low current power supply for helping to drive certain types of transistors).

In the example of a step-down converter (this isn't what is normally in a large switching power supply, but it's a little simpler explanation), you have an inductor feeding the output. By its nature, it likes to maintain a steady current and needs to absorb or release energy to change its current. It's like a capacitor for current instead of voltage, in a way.

So if one end of the inductor goes to the load and feeds the output current, the other end goes to a source that's either at 0V or at a higher-than-output voltage (the "switching" part of a switching power supply refers to something switching these voltages).

Well, when the source is at a higher voltage, the inductor current speeds up, and when it's at a lower voltage it slows down, but if you switch fast enough you can maintain it arbitrarily close to a desired level.

Capacitors are used in the output of most supplies with varying loads because they react basically as fast as possible (but also make the power supply less quick to alter its output voltage - but good thing most don't have to!). Otherwise, delay in the feedback that controls the power supply means sharp changes in load cause big voltage swings at the output, which may disrupt operation or cause damage. The capacitors at the output help stabilize that and only need to last on the timescale the power supply needs to readjust its current output.

V/I=R

2.1/.0062=338 ohms.

They did it emulating a specific architecture on an 8-bit microcontroller. The microcontroller actually isn't a terrible architecture but it's a far cry from the architecture they were emulating, and it's missing things an operating system would need like a large address space, memory management unit, etc.

I can't speak to how they emulated it internally in their project as I haven't investigated the source code, but I know they used a programming language to write it in. I would expect to find a lot of switch statements based on parts of the instruction opcodes.

The way my project worked is I organized opcode fields into 4-bit fields which branch into one of 16 different spots in the emulator. There's a trick in a specific microcontroller where you can take an opcode byte, multiply it by 16, and then use the low result byte as a calculated jump, or nibble swap the high byte (in the same step that loads it to the working register) and do the same sort of 16-way jump.

So my emulation works out to doing 1 of 16 things, between 3 and 6 times in a row (though the sets of things differ between steps). I totally avoid having tables of jump offsets and things like that. The downside is that each "phrase" of code is only 8 instructions long at maximum, because instructions are 2 bytes and I was stuck with 16-byte long sections without adding more instructions to make the spacing farther apart in the calculated jump. If I needed more than 8 instructions, I needed to find an unused area in a table and jump to that to finish up.

So the quick run-through of emulation of one instruction looks like this: First, the instruction is fetched, either from RAM or flash memory depending on the address. After that, operand A and operand B are evaluated, even if they're not actually used (these both use the fancy 16-way branching).

The selectors for those operands comprise one of the instruction bytes. The other byte contains an operation code and a suboperation code. The operation is executed (this uses another 16-way branch) - and for a simple arithmetic operation, this actually performs an addition, subtraction, multiplication, or logic operation between virtual registers. For those kinds of operations, the suboperation is responsible for storing the result back to a register (it picks which register), or pushing a byte or word result to the stack is also a valid destination. If a stack destination is used, there's another 16-way branch performed to check if that memory page (there are 16 of them) is allowed to be written.

So you can see I used that trick a LOT. It makes the interpreter compact due to code reuse (i.e., the operation is always the same code no matter which suboperation you pick after it and is only present in the emulator once) and very performant because you're not looking up jump offsets and playing a lot of games to figure out what code needs to run next.

The most complicated instructions follow this kind of execution chain: Instruction fetch, Operand A and B lookup (2 phrases executed), operation (atomic read-modify-write operation class, where the "operation" code just helps set up a memory address, this is the third phrase executed), then a memory protection test is run to make sure the selected address is writable (fourth phrase), then the atomic read-modify-write sub-operation is run (fifth phrase), and one of the atomic read-modify-write sub-ops only uses one of the operands... the unused one is used to branch into yet another phrase table which executes one final instruction that actually does the intended operation, then a final return out of emulation. Somehow all that complexity actually fits in 68 instruction cycles, 4 of which are the initial call instruction into emulation, and the return from it.

A half adder adds two single digit binary numbers and provides a two digit binary number as a result (because it takes two digits to represent a "2").

The term half adder is used because it lacks a necessary component to connect multiple adders together for adding larger binary numbers - specifically, a carry input.

In contrast, a full adder allows you to add three binary numbers: one digit from the first operand, one digit from the second operand, and the carry output from the less significant bit (the previous adder in the sequence). You still only require two outputs since a two digit result is adequate to represent a "3". The less significant output digit is the result bit, while the more significant one is the carry out that would be passed to the higher order bits if another adder were connected in that direction.

Let's compare a capacitor and a chemical battery.

A capacitor will store useful charge at any voltage; if you can feed it 1.6V, it will charge up to 1.6V, and that voltage directly relates to the energy inside it. If you could only give it 1.4V, it will still charge up to that point and have a vaguely similar (but less) stored energy.

Chemical batteries are a little different. Let's look at, for example, a nickel-metal hydride cell - up to around a volt or so, there is very very little energy contained in them. That is to say, it takes only a little charge to get them up to a volt. The bulk of their energy comes in as they cross around the 1.2V area; the voltage will stay in that range through most of the charge. When they start to get full, the voltage will increase faster up to 1.5-1.6V.

So the moral of the story is that on one of those cells, if you're only feeding it 1V, you really can't charge it effectively. If you've got 1.2V, you'll get partway there but still nowhere close to what 1.4V would get you.

4.8V sounds like either a nickel-cadmium or nickel-metal hydride chemistry - you will probably want 3 solar cells in series, or a boost converter.

Nickel-cadmium can handle over-charge current pretty well, and supplying 4 battery cells with 3 solar cells (~6.5V peak) isn't unreasonable; if cells are charged in an imbalanced way, the overcharged ones will pass overcharge current (generating heat instead of filling up the battery) and allow the undercharged ones to catch up. As long as the solar cells aren't pumping too much current, the batteries will be okay (I'll leave this exact research to you; there are lots of references out on the internet!)

For nickel-metal hydride, overcharge will eventually damage the batteries. Some small overcharge current is okay, but beyond that, damage will accumulate. Because of this, on simple designs, you tend to either use small enough (current wise) solar cells that the overcharge current can be absorbed more or less safely, or you want to aim your final voltage a little more conservatively. 1.4V/cell (5.6V on a 4.8V pack) is probably a safe compromise that will let you get most of the battery capacity without causing excessive damage.

On lithium-ion batteries, the difficulties get worse. These batteries can't safely pass over-charge current, so you need to strictly stick to a max voltage (and also minimum voltage!) on each cell, and if cells aren't charged equally, this gets complicated. Very strongly recommended design practice is to monitor the voltage of each cell individually and not allow them to over or under charge. Charging a series string of lithium-ion cells, where the charger only connects to the end cells is generally considered unsafe. You need connections from the charger to spots between each cell for the individual cells to be properly monitored.

Pump: make sure both intake and return tube are in the liquid to prevent splashing. If you want to speed control it, use a 12V PWM style motor speed controller or a buck converter rated to a bit more than 3A (you could get away with less if you only run it at a low enough current through the converter) - a resistor will heat up and/or need a big heatsink (but it would work).

Fans: Wire in parallel, along with the speed controller or pump.

If you want less airflow, you could wire the fans in series with each other with a small capacitor (say, 22uF) between ground and the midpoint connection between the fans to help stabilize the voltage a bit, if they're not happy running without it.

By utilizing both these techniques, you could probably get the current draw down to about an amp and a half, which would last quite a while on a car battery.
